Why another blog?

While writing this section I notices an interesting contradiction. The tldr is significantly more consumable but I’m choosing to publish an obtuse academic adjacent essay instead. Clearly I don’t care about making my ideas easy to understand but I’m publishing this essay in hopes that regardless people will engage with it.

tldr: it’s an opportunity for auto-critique and self-reflection.

This is an honest and succinct answer to the titular question, however, in the spirit of self-reflection, I want to discuss why exactly this introspective activity is good and why writing is my medium of choice for facilitating it.

This essay will being with an analysis of Pixar’s Wall-E which I will try to extend to a discussion on content consumption in general. Finally since I am trying to justify a normative claim, I will finish my argument by introducing some conflicting ideas of Aristotle and Nietzsche.

Wall-E, complacency and duty

Wall-E is a movie which can not be rewatched enough! I’ve maybe watched it upwards of 5 times at this point and I can honestly say that I’ve gotten something completely different out of each viewing. On my most recent viewing, the theme of complacency was especially resonant. Auto distracting the passengers by changing the colors of their clothes or by giving a free cupcake during the ships anniversary paralleled some of the ways I feel I’ve been caught up with the mechanical actions of living (cooking, meeting friends, working). It’s too easy to watch Wall-E, then like the passengers aboard Axiom, ignore what that little rusty robot has to say, and get pulled back in to rhythm of living. This is the moment where I felt Aristotle’s Nicomachean ethics begging to be introduced.

Another idea that really stuck with by me was eve’s evolving relationship to Wall-E and her directive. After first meeting Wall-E and becoming friends, her programming prioritizes the retrieval of the “extraterrestrial vegetation” above all else. While nearing the end of the movie in the trash compactor aboard the axiom, Eve turns away from the plant, and thus her directive, because Wall-E is injured. The movie offers Eve convenient solution to both problems by returning to earth which fulfils her missions and secures spare parts for Wall-E. This leads two contradictory interpretations: While writing this section I was tempted to think about this through the lens of Maslow’s theory of hierarchy. Maslow writes about the need for self-actualization “[Discontent will occur] unless the individual is doing what he is fitted for”. That, all humans are social creatures and so fitted for participating faithfully in society, follows from Maslow’s arguments which implies performing our social obligations is a necessary precondition for personal fulfilment.

  1. Wall-E is a kids movie and in real life you need to choose between personal fulfilment and our duty towards society
  2. Wall-E was on to something and to be personally fulfilled, we must simultaneously achieve personal goals and fulfil out societal duties.

But regardless of which interpretation is more compelling, complacency always seems to be the enemy of social obligation. In the first interpretation, it manifests itself as a level of selfish comfort, allowing people to ignore their duty towards people without the same level of comfort. In the second interpretation, complacency manifests itself, like in Wall-E, as monotonous existence without any true fulfilment (this sentiment is best echoed by Captain McCrea when he says “I don’t want to survive, I want to live”).
